title: Iceberg internals: metadata, snapshots, commits
summary: How an Iceberg table is really a tree of immutable metadata files, how readers prune with it, and how writers commit safely with an atomic pointer swap.

blocks.text: Chapter 21 explained why a directory of Parquet files is not a table. In Iceberg a table is a tree of immutable metadata files, and the only mutable thing is one pointer held by the catalog. Time travel, safe concurrent writes, fast planning and maintenance all follow from this tree.
22.1 The metadata tree

Reading an Iceberg table always starts at the catalog and walks down. Each level is a separate file in object storage, and each level carries enough summary information to skip whole branches of the level below.

head: Level
Format
What it holds
Written when
rows: Format version, UUID, location, schemas, partition specs, sort orders, properties, snapshots, refs
A new file on every commit
One row per manifest: path, spec id, content (data or deletes), file counts, partition bounds
One row per file: path, partition tuple, record count, size, per-column null counts and lower/upper bounds, status (ADDED/EXISTING/DELETED)
When files change; reused across snapshots

blocks.text: The key word is *reuse*: an append writes one new manifest and a manifest list pointing to it **plus all old manifests unchanged**, so commit cost scales with the change, not the table.
22.2 Snapshots and the table metadata file

A snapshot is the complete state of the table at one moment: the set of live data and delete files, reachable through exactly one manifest list. The `metadata.json` file stores the list of snapshots that have not been expired, each with an id, parent id, sequence number, timestamp, schema id, manifest list location and a summary (operation such as `append`, `overwrite`, `delete` or `replace`, plus counts of added and removed files and records).

The metadata file also stores `refs`: named pointers to snapshots. `main` is the default branch that ordinary reads use; other branches and tags are covered in chapter 23. Old metadata files and snapshots stay in storage until cleaned up, so time travel and rollback just follow an older pointer.

blocks.title: Abridged metadata.json

blocks.text: From format v2, each commit gets an increasing data sequence number. Equality deletes apply only to data files with a lower sequence number, position deletes to lower or equal. That is how a later delete targets earlier rows without rewriting them.
22.3 Planning a query: pruning with statistics
Planning `WHERE order_date = '2026-11-01' AND customer_id = 42` lists no directories; it walks the tree and prunes at each level:

items: Read the current `metadata.json` (one small GET) and find the current snapshot.
Read the manifest list. Manifests whose partition bounds exclude `2026-11-01` are skipped unopened.
Read the remaining manifests and drop files whose partition tuple or `customer_id` bounds exclude the predicate.
Hand surviving files (plus applicable delete files) to the engine, which can still prune Parquet row groups.

blocks.text: Stats are only as good as the layout: if `customer_id` is scattered randomly, every file's min/max covers almost everything. Sorting on filter columns (chapter 25) turns stats into skipped bytes.

For very wide tables, limit column metrics with the `write.metadata.metrics.*` table properties (truncate string bounds, disable metrics for columns nobody filters on). Stats for hundreds of columns make manifests large and planning slow.
22.4 Committing: optimistic concurrency and the atomic swap
Iceberg has no lock server. Writers are optimistic: do all the work assuming no one else writes, then publish atomically and check the assumption.

steps.label: Swap
steps.sub: catalog: if current == v41 then set v42

blocks.text: The atomic step is a catalog compare-and-swap: 'point to v42 only if still at v41'. Implementations differ (chapter 24); on success the commit is visible to every reader at once; on failure nothing visible changed and the new files are simply unreferenced.
Conflicts and retries

On failure the writer refreshes and checks whether its change is still valid on the new base. An append almost never conflicts: it rebuilds the manifest list, reusing its manifests, and retries. An overwrite, delete or MERGE validates: did a concurrent commit add or remove files it read? Under serializable isolation new matching data files cause a conflict; under snapshot isolation only concurrent deletes of the same data do. A failed validation throws and the job must rerun.
Retries are bounded by table properties such as `commit.retry.num-retries` (check the current documentation for defaults).

Many writers committing every few seconds to one table spend their time retrying: `CommitFailedException`, rising commit latency, orphan files from abandoned attempts. The fix is architectural: fewer, larger commits, or one committing job per table.
22.5 Format versions v1, v2 and v3
The format version, recorded in the metadata file, is a promise about which features readers must understand.

head: Version
Main additions
Practical meaning
rows: Snapshots, manifests, hidden partitioning, schema evolution
Position and equality delete files, data sequence numbers
Merge-on-read for updates, deletes, CDC. Today's common baseline.
Deletion vectors (Puffin), new types (variant, nanosecond timestamps, geospatial), default values, row lineage
Engine support varies: check the current documentation of every engine that touches the table.

blocks.text: Upgrading the format version is one-way in practice. If any reader cannot read v3, the upgrade breaks it. Inventory readers first.
22.6 What lives in storage, and why it grows

Paths under `data/` and `metadata/` are only a writer convention. Every file is referenced by its full path in a manifest, so readers infer nothing from directories; that is why partitioning can change without moving data.

Every commit adds files: a metadata JSON, a manifest list, at least one manifest, plus data. One commit per minute means over 1,400 snapshots a day. Old metadata JSON files can be cleaned automatically (`write.metadata.delete-after-commit.enabled`, `write.metadata.previous-versions-max`), but snapshots and the data only they reference stay until expired (chapter 25).

blocks.title: Diagnosing slow planning on a CDC table
blocks.text: A team commits Postgres CDC into an Iceberg table every two minutes. After three months, point lookups spend 40 seconds in planning. The `manifests` metadata table shows about 9,000 small manifests and no snapshot has ever been expired.
items: Planning opened thousands of Avro files, each a GET of tens of milliseconds.
Rewriting manifests and expiring snapshots brought planning under a second; compacting data and delete files fixed scan time.

blocks.title: Design the commit path for three writers
blocks.text: Three jobs write one `events` table: a stream appending every 60 seconds, a nightly GDPR delete job, and an hourly MERGE for late records. Which pairs can conflict, what should each do on a failed commit, and how would you restructure them to keep retries rare?
hints: Which operations only add files, and which validate against concurrent changes?
Could partitioning by event date reduce overlap?

items: An Iceberg table is a tree: catalog pointer -> metadata.json -> manifest list -> manifests -> data and delete files.
All files are immutable; the catalog pointer is the only mutable state, and swapping it is the commit.
Manifest lists and manifests carry partition and column statistics so planners prune without listing directories.
Commits are optimistic: write everything, then compare-and-swap; on conflict, refresh, validate and retry.
Format v2 adds row-level deletes and sequence numbers; v3 adds deletion vectors and new types; upgrade only when all readers support it.

blocks.q: What exactly happens at the moment an Iceberg commit becomes visible to readers?
options: All manifests are rewritten to include the new files
The catalog atomically swaps the table's metadata pointer from the expected old metadata file to the new one
The writer renames a temporary directory to the table directory
The writer updates the existing metadata.json in place
blocks.explain: Visibility is one compare-and-swap of the catalog pointer. Nothing is updated in place, and directory renames are what Iceberg avoids: they are not atomic on object stores.

blocks.q: A query filters on `customer_id = 42`; the table is partitioned only by day. Where can Iceberg still skip files?
options: In the manifests, using per-file lower and upper bounds for customer_id
In the catalog, which indexes column values
Nowhere; without a partition on customer_id every file must be read
Only in the manifest list, using partition summaries
blocks.explain: Manifests store per-file column bounds, so files whose range excludes 42 are dropped. Manifest-list summaries only cover partition fields; the catalog holds no column stats.

blocks.q: Two jobs commit at the same time: an append and a MERGE that read the same partition. The append wins the swap. What happens to the MERGE under serializable isolation?
options: It retries blindly with no checks
It refreshes, validates against the new snapshot, finds new data files matching its read set, and fails with a conflict
It waits on a lock held by the append
blocks.explain: Serializable validation fails when a concurrent commit added files the MERGE should have read. There is no lock to wait on, and a blind overwrite would lose data.

blocks.q: Why can an append-only commit to a 50 TB table be cheap?
options: Because snapshots are not created for appends
Because the catalog stores the file list and only appends a row
Because Iceberg appends rows into existing Parquet files
Because the new manifest list reuses all existing manifests and only adds a new one for the new files
blocks.explain: Manifests are shared between snapshots, so the commit writes one manifest, one manifest list and one metadata file. Parquet files are never modified, and appends do create snapshots.
